notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on 1 Kings 6. I didn't find material for every verse or every tradition, and I've listed the gaps at the end.

---

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1 (the date)**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says the 480 years show how long Israel lived in the land without a temple. God's conditional promise to Solomon (vv. 11-13) depended on obedience is a later point. On the date itself, he reckons that the Exodus took place in 1447 b.c. He also says Solomon probably started planning in his first year, since preparing the timber may have taken three years. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Constable reckons that Solomon began temple construction about 966 B.C. According to this verse the Exodus took place in 1445 or 1446 B.C. Most conservative scholars who take statements in Scripture like this verse seriously hold this date. He notes that some respected conservative scholars, such as Kenneth Kitchen, prefer a later date of about 1280 BC. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html
- Pett links the date to the land finally being at rest: the period of wandering, and of having a temporary, travelling sanctuary, was considered to be over. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/1-kings-6.html
- A Bible Hub study note says Ziv falls after Passover, linking the temple's construction to Israel's deliverance and God's faithfulness. — https://biblehub.com/study/1_kings/6-1.htm

**v. 2 (size)**
- Guzik: with a cubit of about 18 inches, the temple was about 90 × 30 × 45 feet. That is not large for an ancient temple, but its glory was not in its size. He says it followed the tabernacle's design at twice the size, so Solomon meant it as a continuation of the tabernacle. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Constable: it faced east like the tabernacle, and was similar to other ancient Near Eastern temples in both size and design. This is an example of acculturation: God giving revelation of Himself in forms that were familiar to the original recipients. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html
- Hawker points to 1 Chronicles 28:11–12: God gave David the pattern before he died. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/1-kings-6.html

**v. 3 (portico)** Guzik: the porch, or vestibule, stood on the east side. It was about 30 feet wide and 15 feet deep, and the same height as the main building. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/

**v. 4 (windows)**
- Constable: these were narrow clerestory windows set above the three storeys of side rooms. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia thinks they were mainly for fresh air and to let incense smoke escape, since many lamps lit the hall. The Holy of Holies seems to have had no windows and was always enveloped in darkness. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14499a.htm

**vv. 5–6 (side rooms and ledges)**
- Guzik: the side rooms ran along the north, south and west sides in three storeys. They stood against the temple but were not structurally part of it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Constable: the priests used them for storage and service. The rooms got wider on each higher floor, and the offset ledges held up the upper floors so no beams had to go into the temple walls. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html
- The Biblical Illustrator draws a lesson: as it ascended in height, so it still was wider and wider. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-kings-6.html

**v. 7 (no iron tool heard)**
- Guzik sees three lessons. God's work is done by human hands, yet Solomon wanted it to show that the temple was of God and not of man. The greatest work often happens quietly, though only because of hard work at the quarry. And, quoting Adam Clarke, souls must be "squared and fitted" here on earth for heaven. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Constable thinks Solomon wanted to keep the site holy even during building, and links the verse to Deuteronomy 27:5–6. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html
- Matthew Poole and Benson give three reasons: easier transport, the splendour of the work, and a spiritual meaning. Poole says the church should be free of contention, and that no one enters the heavenly temple without first being "hewed and squared." Keil and Delitzsch explain that the Hebrew word means stones fully finished at the quarry. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/6-7.htm
- Gill, citing Josephus, says the stones were so finely joined that no tool marks could be seen. Clarke says only mallets were needed, to drive in the joints and pins. — https://studylight.org/bible/cev/1-kings/6-7.html
- Spurgeon and Henry Morris, quoted by Precept Austin, see the silent building as a picture of the spiritual temple the Holy Spirit is building now. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-6-commentary
- Matthew Henry: the stones of the heavenly building must be hewn and squared by divine grace, and so made meet for a place there. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-6.html

**vv. 8–10** Guzik says these verses describe the three-storey side rooms around the north, west and south sides. He calls cedar one of the finest building materials available. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/

**vv. 11–13 (God's word to Solomon)**
- Guzik: the promise was conditional on obedience and mostly renewed what God had said at Sinai. He stresses that God said He would dwell "among" Israel, not "in" the temple the way pagans thought their gods lived in temples. The temple was a place for people to meet God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Constable: the promise depended on keeping the Mosaic covenant. Because Solomon did not, the kingdom was divided. The writer placed this word in the middle of the building account to emphasize the centrality of obedience. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html
- Dale Ralph Davis, quoted by Precept Austin, notes that the "you" is singular. Solomon's personal fidelity to Yahweh's covenant law is the condition for Yahweh's gracious presence, and he applies this to church leaders. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-6-commentary
- Matthew Henry: God noticed what Solomon was doing, and None employ themselves for God without having his eye upon them. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-6.html
- The Biblical Illustrator: gold and cedar could not enclose and secure a purely spiritual presence. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-kings-6.html

**v. 14** Precept Austin notes that this is the second of three statements that the work was finished (vv. 9, 14, 38). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-6-commentary
The Biblical Illustrator praises the fact that Solomon not only began the house but finished it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-kings-6.html

**vv. 15–18 (cedar lining, Most Holy Place)** Hawker compares the cedar walls and golden floor with Solomon's carriage in Song of Songs 3:9–10, and sees the temple as a picture of Christ. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/1-kings-6.html

**vv. 19–20 (inner sanctuary, altar)**
- Guzik: the Most Holy Place was a 30-foot cube covered entirely in gold. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Constable: the "altar" is the altar of incense in the holy place. He leaves open why this room was 20 cubits high when the building was 30: perhaps a raised floor, a lower ceiling, or a room within a room. We do not know. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia concludes there must have been a 10-cubit space above the inner sanctuary. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14499a.htm
- Pett thinks the altar was stone, cased in cedar and then gold, and was seen as belonging to the Most Holy Place (compare Hebrews 9:3–4). — https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/1-kings-6.html

**vv. 21–22 (gold and chains)**
- Guzik, quoting Patterson and Austel: the gold chains across the front strengthened the sense that the Most Holy Place could not be entered. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Precept Austin sets out how different translations render the chains and links the veil to the high priest's once-a-year entry (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-6-commentary
- Matthew Henry: the gold was not a thin wash. Solomon spared no expense. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-6.html
- Pett says the repetition is typical of ancient writing and was meant to stress how generous Solomon was. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/1-kings-6.html

**vv. 23–28 (two cherubim)**
- Guzik: the two large figures faced the entrance, so the high priest saw these guardians as soon as he entered. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Constable: these were two extra, freestanding cherubim, in addition to those on the ark's lid. They may have looked like "winged sphinxes." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html
- Matthew Henry: everything was made new except the ark, Moses' original, as the sign that God's presence does not change whether His people meet in a tent or a temple. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-6.html

**v. 29 (cherubim, palms, flowers)**
- Guzik: these follow the tabernacle, whose inner covering had cherubim woven into it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Ligonier (Reformed): Eden and Solomon's temple were both guarded by cherubim (Gen. 3:24; Ex. 26:31; 1 Kings 6:23–29) and were filled with trees. — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/jesus-is-the-new-temple

**v. 30 (gold floor)** Matthew Henry and Hawker both link it to the New Jerusalem's streets of pure gold (Revelation 21:21). Henry adds: Gold was under foot there, as it should be in all the living temples. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-6.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/1-kings-6.html

**vv. 31–35 (doors)**
- Matthew Henry follows the older reading that the inner doors took up a fifth of the wall and the outer doors a quarter. Both sets were carved with cherubim. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-6.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia describes a five-sided gateway, six cubits wide, through a partition two cubits thick. It says the doors stood open, but a veil always hid the Holy of Holies. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14499a.htm

**v. 36 (inner court)**
- Guzik: this was the court of the priests, where the altar and basin stood. The people worshipped in the outer courts, since under the Old Covenant the temple itself was only for the priests. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Constable: scholars debate how the cedar row related to the stone. It could be cedar on top of the stone, a cedar lining, or alternating rows. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html

**vv. 37–38 (seven years)**
- Constable: Ziv means "flowers" and Bul means "moisture," so the work actually took about seven and a half years. Seven may have suggested a perfect building. The exact site is unknown, but it lay on today's Temple Mount platform. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html
- Guzik: it was easy for Israel to focus on the temple instead of the God of the temple. It was plundered within five years of Solomon's death (1 Kings 14:25–27). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
- Matthew Henry: given its size, the temple was built quickly, because Solomon was in earnest and had many workers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-6.html

---

## Where interpreters differ

The disagreements I found are between individual commentators, not clearly between denominations.

- **Did Solomon follow God's pattern? (vv. 2, 20–28)** Guzik sees the temple as a deliberate continuation of the tabernacle. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/
  Coffman disagrees. He says nothing in the text claims Solomon followed divine instructions. He calls the giant cherubim Solomon's utter disregard of the pattern which God gave Moses. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-6.html
  Pett goes further. Gold everywhere broke the tabernacle's rule that metals grew more precious closer to the Most Holy Place, and the idea came from men, not God. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/1-kings-6.html

- **Did God live "in" the temple? (v. 13)** Chuck Smith says the temple was built as a house for God to dwell in. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/1-kings-6.html
  Guzik says God carefully promised to dwell among Israel, not in the building. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-6/

- **Christ as the true temple, and a future temple** Ligonier (Reformed) says the temple was a shadow pointing to Jesus, and We are not looking for another temple. We have Him. — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/jesus-is-the-new-temple
  Another Ligonier devotional notes that many Christians expect a rebuilt Jerusalem temple, and argues the only temple to look for is Christ's body. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/temple-of-jesus-body
  I did not find a source from the other side of this debate.

---

## Other views

- **The 480 years (v. 1)**
  - Catholic Answers: 480 looks like two symbolic numbers multiplied (12 × 40), and ancient temples were often given symbolic dates. A plain reading of 480 puts the Exodus in the 1400s, but the place-name Raamses points to the 1200s, and most scholars place the Exodus in the 1200s, during the reign of Ramesses II. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/when-was-the-exodus
  - The Holman Bible Dictionary gives the same reasoning about Raamses. — https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hbd/e/exodus.html
  - An older note on StudyLight (the author isn't named) argues that other chronological data, such as Acts 13:20, suggest a period longer than 480 years. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/1-kings/6-1.html
  - A Bible Hub article defends reading the 480 literally. — https://biblehub.com/q/Significance_of_480_years_in_1_Kings_6_1.htm

- **Archaeology** Constable, quoting Eugene Merrill, says a 10th-century BC temple at ʿAin Dara in Syria closely resembles Solomon's, so a temple in Israel at that time "rests on firm ground." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-6.html

- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey)** The article describes the cherubim as winged feline creatures with human faces. It says the cherubim, palms and flowers are reminiscent of the cherubs who guarded the entrance to the Tree of Life. — https://2fdavidson.bibleodyssey.org/articles/first-temple/

- **Catholic**
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia gives the room names (hekal and debir) and says the measurements are inside measurements. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14499a.htm
  - It says the cherubim probably faced the Holy Place. It adds that the title "who sittest upon the Cherubim" is better understood as referring to God's heavenly throne-bearers. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03646c.htm
  - It also explains that "cherub" comes from an Assyrian word meaning "near ones," the beings closest to God. — https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/cherubim
